## Chapter 7: Creating the Right Environment for Data-Aware Design

### Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

Data-driven design aims to diminish reliance on "gut" decision making and consequently breaks traditional hierarchical decision-making structures. The stereotype of management-led, top-down decision making based on hunches cannot flourish in a data-literate environment. Company-wide data literacy—including addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions—invites discussion, challenge, and most importantly the potential to be wrong.

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

The authors argue data is most effective when collected using multiple techniques: A/B testing, ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, and usability research. Grounded and carefully gathered user data drives decisions and represents a less risky prospect than relying on hunches from individual executives. A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield entitled "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO" addresses this issue.

Data serves as an effective way to resolve conflicts in decision making without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. John Ciancutti, who worked at Netflix for several years as VP of Product Engineering, illustrates how data literacy across all roles at Netflix became a source of freedom and innovation within the company.

Patty McCord, who spent over 12 years as Netflix's Chief Talent Officer overseeing talent acquisition and HR, shows how an environment embracing data helps employees. Having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers allows more people to have a voice in product development.

### Netflix's Universal Adoption

One of the things that made the data-driven approach successful at Netflix was that the practice of leveraging data was well established and universally accepted throughout the company. It may have started at the top with Reed Hastings (CEO) and Neil Hunt (CPO) driving and believing in the value of leveraging data, but it was also embraced by everyone from management to individual contributors on the team.

Patty McCord points out that at Netflix, unlike some companies where the CEO might get to do whatever he wants, executives are not exempt from data-driven processes. A common tendency exists where any employee, including executives, can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. Embracing A/B testing helps mitigate this top-down approach because everyone can learn from experimentation.

### Leadership Accountability in Practice

When Reed Hastings engaged in product testing and had a strong idea for what he wanted to see in the product, he would submit his ideas to the same rigor of A/B testing as everyone else in the product team. On rare occasions, Reed might dictate the exact way a product idea would work, but he would do this on "his test cell"—the experimental group in the test that he was backing. This cell would be tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, then it didn't get launched.

Having upper-level management hold themselves accountable to the same process as individual teams reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation and to the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome. This value was central to how the company worked.

### Shifting Organizational Mindset

If trying to shift into a data-aware framework, it is critical to examine how product and design decisions have been made to date. If these decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, it is worth ensuring those people can understand and recognize the value of bringing user/customer data into the decision-making process because their weight may be diminished—as is the weight of any individual opinion. Designers should check whether they themselves are comfortable and willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of their own opinion within the design and product development process.
